problem: Frodsham's translation says the ship was held at Hong Kong to repair damage from a collision with a merchant paddle-steamer, not storm damage; the school passage describes halls arranged so one master could oversee about a hundred pupils, not a 'strict timetable'. fix.digest: While the Travancore was repaired after a paddle-steamer struck her in the harbour, Guo toured the Government Central School, noting how its halls were laid out so that one master could watch about a hundred pupils, and next day the gaol, whose cleanliness, chapel, hospital and equal treatment of prisoners of every nationality he praised. He also noted how fast the colony had grown.

problem: Days are swapped. Per Frodsham and BiblioAsia, on 13 Dec Guo met Governor Jervois, visited Whampoa's house and garden and inspected Fort Canning (fortifications, barracks, guns); the Yangwu salute and drill were on 14 Dec. No source seen says the fort's layout struck him as unlike a Chinese fort.

fix.headline: Whampoa's garden and Fort Canning
fix.digest: The ship docked about eleven in the morning in rain. Guo was taken to the house and garden of the merchant Hoo Ah Kay (Whampoa), who would become the first Qing consul in Singapore, met Governor Jervois at Government House, and inspected the fortifications, barracks and guns of Fort Canning.

problem: Whampoa's garden belongs to 13 Dec; the 14th was the day of the Yangwu salute and drill, the Botanic Gardens, Judge Ford's court and a second call on Jervois (Frodsham; BiblioAsia).

fix.headline: A Qing corvette and a colonial court
fix.digest: In rain and thunder Guo boarded the Fuzhou-built corvette Yangwu, whose crew manned the yards, fired a salute and drilled; he visited the Botanic Gardens, sat beside Judge Theodore Ford at a hearing, and called again on Governor Jervois before sailing. Liu, by contrast, left no impression of the town.

problem: In Frodsham the sightseeing (prison, Buddhist temples, a sold former royal palace), the reflection on how Europeans hold such countries, and the change to the Peshawur all fall on 22 Dec (GX 2/11/7); 21 Dec is only the arrival.

fix.digest: After visiting a prison, Buddhist temples and a former royal palace that had been sold, Guo reflected that Europeans held countries like Ceylon less by soldiers than by planning, settlement and trade, taking control without overthrowing the local ruling house. The same day the party changed to the P&O Peshawur.

problem: The Ceylon reflection is in the 22 Dec entry (GX 2/11/7), per Frodsham.

problem: BiblioAsia's caption describes the item as a Victorian poem whose illustration shows Guo as a monkey in Chinese dress gazing at the British lion; the 'errand of apology' theme is not in the source seen. Report the stereotype plainly as what was printed.

fix.digest: Punch ran a comic poem on the Chinese envoy's arrival; as reproduced by BiblioAsia, its illustration showed Guo as a monkey in Chinese dress gazing fondly at the British lion. It was the satirical frame through which many readers first met Guo.

problem: Li Jiaqi quotes the letter: Li had heard from Zhou Xiaotang that He Jinshou had memorialised asking that the book be destroyed, and notes the Yamen had printed it in movable type.

fix.digest: Writing to his elder brother Li Hanzhang, Li reported news that He Jinshou had memorialised asking for the envoy's book to be destroyed, after the Zongli Yamen had printed it in movable type. The editors of his letters misdated this one to 1878.

problem: Li Jiaqi says Li Ciming copied two passages of the diary matching those He Jinshou cited and blamed the Zongli Yamen for publishing it; the phrase 'praised the barbarians beyond all measure' as the diarist's words is not in the source.

fix.digest: Li Ciming copied into his diary two passages of Guo's book, the same ones He Jinshou's memorial had cited, and blamed the Zongli Yamen for having it printed. The private diary shows the official objection taken up by literati opinion.

problem: The Paper says the cloak was the brown cloak of the British admiral (提督) guiding the tour of 甲敦炮台 in southern England (fort unidentified), and, as read here, that the cloak, Brazil and concert complaints were raised in Liu's earlier quarrels rather than listed in the formal ten-count memorial. Hedge the link to the formal charges.

fix.digest: On a tour of a fort (甲敦炮台) in southern England, the British admiral guiding the party draped his own cloak over Guo against the cold; Liu objected that an envoy should not wear foreign clothes even if he froze, and the two quarrelled. Liu later used the cloak against him.

problem: The Wikisource entry (GX 3/8/2) says Li Shuchang (Li Chunzhai) and others described two days of questioning with Liu, whose accusations Guo called wildly absurd; questioning of Liu's servant Sheng Kui (盛奎) some days earlier had shown that an anonymous letter was Liu's forgery. The 8/4 entry calls Liu a 'false envoy' (伪使) and says Guo had suffered much from him without any help; the phrase 'harm and no benefit' is not in the text.

fix.digest: Li Shuchang and others described two days of confrontation with Liu, whose accusations, built on Beijing gossip, Guo called wildly absurd; and questioning of Liu's servant Sheng Kui had shown that an anonymous letter was Liu's own forgery. Two days later Guo called his deputy a false envoy from whom he had suffered much and gained no help at all.
